title: Intel’s Tiny Bridges Could Lead to Very Big Paychecks
gist: Daniel Nenni argues Intel's advanced packaging (EMIB, EMIB-T, Foveros) could become a meaningful standalone growth engine by stitching together other companies' AI chiplets, and serves as a lower-commitment on-ramp to Intel Foundry. He stresses the 'billions' are potential, not established revenue, citing a roadmap to 16+ HBM stacks by 2028 and Seok-Hee Lee's June 2026 appointment, with yield, thermal and reliability as key hurdles.

insights.claim: Intel does not need to design winning AI chips to benefit from AI infrastructure spending because it can supply the advanced packaging connections that make other companies' designs work.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Gives Intel an AI exposure path independent of its own processor competitiveness.
insights.quote: Intel does not need to design every winning AI chip to benefit from AI infrastructure spending.

insights.claim: Intel's packaging services can integrate chiplets made on different technologies and foundries, letting customers buy a specific capability without committing every component to Intel's wafer fabs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Packaging lowers switching cost for foundry customers, widening Intel's addressable market.

insights.claim: Intel has described customers approaching first for advanced packaging, with successful execution building confidence in its broader foundry services, making packaging a land-and-expand entry point.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Packaging wins could be a leading indicator of future Intel wafer foundry deals.
insights.quote: Packaging offers another way to begin working together.

insights.claim: The billions in potential packaging revenue for Intel are not established revenue; outcomes depend on actual design wins, volumes, pricing, investment and operating costs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Investors should track concrete design wins rather than headline TAM.
insights.quote: The billions in the headline represent potential, rather than established packaging revenue.

insights.claim: EMIB uses small silicon bridges embedded in the package substrate to connect neighbouring chips, concentrating dense connections where needed rather than using a large silicon interposer, which Intel argues offers cost, flexibility and scaling advantages.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: EMIB is Intel's cost-differentiated alternative to full-interposer approaches.
insights.locator: This is where Intel's alphabet soup

insights.claim: Foveros enables vertical stacking of chiplets, while EMIB-T adds connections through its bridges to improve power delivery and support higher bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Combining lateral and vertical integration broadens Intel's packaging menu for AI systems.
insights.quote: Think of EMIB as connecting buildings across a neighborhood and Foveros as adding floors.

insights.claim: Intel's packaging roadmap targets configurations accommodating at least sixteen high-bandwidth memory stacks by 2028, though these remain forward-looking development targets.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Signals the scale of AI accelerator packages Intel aims to serve.
insights.quote: including configurations accommodating at least sixteen high-bandwidth memory stacks by 2028

insights.claim: Building everything into one gigantic chip becomes increasingly difficult and expensive, so AI processors are split into chiplets made on suitable technologies and connected in one package, making the interconnects central to product capability.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for advanced packaging demand across the industry.
insights.locator: The logic starts with a practical problem

insights.claim: In June 2026, Intel appointed semiconductor veteran Seok-Hee Lee to lead advanced packaging, system integration and related manufacturing, signalling packaging is a focused business priority.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Dedicated leadership suggests Intel is treating packaging as a P&L-relevant business.
insights.locator: Intel has also given the effort

insights.claim: Intel's complex packages must meet demanding yield, heat management, testing and reliability standards, and customers need confidence Intel can deliver consistently at production scale.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Execution at scale is the key risk to the packaging thesis.
